# Laser diode principle and optical gain {#sec-ld-principle} [![Open in Colab](https://colab.research.google.com/assets/colab-badge.svg)](https://colab.research.google.com/github/{{< var github_user >}}/{{< var repo >}}/blob/main/{{< var subdir >}}/notebooks/ld-principle.ipynb){.colab-link}  Run this chapter's code in Google Colab (no installation). *Slides 89–91 (degenerately doped pn junction, population inversion under forward bias, gain versus photon energy) and 128–130 (optical gain curve, gain spectra of InGaAsP versus carrier density, peak gain versus carrier density).* ## Key relations In a semiconductor the "two levels" are two bands. Under forward bias, electrons injected into the conduction band and holes in the valence band each reach their own equilibrium, described by the **quasi-Fermi levels** $E_{Fn}$ and $E_{Fp}$ of Chapter 3, with $E_{Fn}-E_{Fp}=eV$ (slide 90). A photon of energy $h\nu$ connects a conduction state $E_2$ with a valence state $E_1$ with $E_2-E_1=h\nu$. Stimulated emission beats absorption when the upper state is more likely full than the lower state, $f_c(E_2)>f_v(E_1)$, which reduces to the **Bernard–Duraffourg condition** $$ E_g d.g > m.g ? d : m, data[0]); return {data, Fn, Fp, dF, pk, Eg: S.Eg}; } Plot.plot({ width: Math.min(width, 1050), height: 320, x: {label: gp.axis === "photon energy" ? "E" : "lam", y: d => Math.max(d.g, 0), fill: "#1baf7a", fillOpacity: 0.3}), Plot.line(gpOut.data, {x: gp.axis === "photon energy" ? EFn − Ec = ${(1000*gpOut.Fn).toFixed(1)} meV · Ev − EFp = ${(1000*gpOut.Fp).toFixed(1)} meV · ΔF = EFn − EFp = ${gpOut.dF.toFixed(4)} eV (red) vs Eg = ${gpOut.Eg} eV (blue) → ${gpOut.dF > gpOut.Eg ? html`gain from ${gpOut.Eg.toFixed(3)} to ${gpOut.dF.toFixed(3)} eV, peak ${gpOut.pk.g.toFixed(0)} cm⁻¹ at ${gpOut.pk.E.toFixed(3)} eV (${gpOut.pk.lam.toFixed(0)} nm)` : html`no gain: ΔF < Eg`}
` ``` Things to try: lower the temperature to 10 K and the gain edge at $\Delta F$ becomes vertical, as in the $T=0$ sketch of slide 91. Compare GaAs with InGaAsP at the same density: the lighter electron mass of InGaAsP fills the conduction band faster, but the heavy holes barely move $E_{Fp}$. The valence band is the bottleneck of inversion in all III–V lasers. ## Gain spectra and peak gain (slides 129–130) ::: {#cell-fig-gain-spectra .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} E = np.linspace(1.40, 1.56, 600) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.8)) for i, n in enumerate((1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0)): g = lz.gain_spectrum_bulk(E, n*1e24, "GaAs")/100 ax.plot(E, g, color=plt.cm.viridis(i/4), label=f"n = {n}×10¹⁸ cm⁻³ (ΔF = {lz.delta_F(n*1e24):.3f} eV)") ax.axhline(0, color=lz.INK2, lw=1); ax.axvline(1.424, color=lz.PALETTE[0], ls="--", lw=1) ax.set(xlabel="photon energy (eV)", ylabel="g (cm⁻¹)", ylim=(-1500, 1800)); ax.legend(fontsize=8); plt.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Free-carrier gain spectra of GaAs at 300 K for injected densities from 1.0 to 3.0×10¹⁸ cm⁻³ (no broadening). As on slide 129, the gain band widens and its peak moves to higher photon energy with n.](ld-principle_files/figure-html/fig-gain-spectra-output-1.png){#fig-gain-spectra width=747 height=391} ::: ::: ::: {#cell-fig-peak-gain .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.5, 3.8)) for (k, (x, y)), c in zip(lz.PEAK_GAIN_SLIDE.items(), (lz.PALETTE[2], lz.PALETTE[0], lz.PALETTE[7])): xx = np.linspace(x[0], x[-1], 50) ax.semilogy(xx, lz.peak_gain_slide(xx*1e18, k), color=c, label=k + " (slide 130)") nn = np.linspace(1.2, 3.0, 25); E = np.linspace(1.40, 1.60, 500) for b, ls in ((0, "--"), (0.03, ":")): pk = [lz.gain_spectrum_bulk(E, n*1e24, broadening=b).max()/100 for n in nn] ax.semilogy(nn, np.where(np.array(pk) > 1, pk, np.nan), ls, color=lz.PALETTE[2], lw=1.5, label=f"GaAs model, broadening {b*1000:.0f} meV") ax.set(xlabel="carrier density n (10¹⁸ cm⁻³)", ylabel="peak gain (cm⁻¹)", ylim=(10, 3000), xlim=(0, 3.1)); ax.legend(fontsize=7.5); plt.show() from scipy.optimize import brentq n_tr = brentq(lambda n: lz.delta_F(n*1e24) - 1.424, 0.3, 3) print(f"model transparency density (ΔF = Eg): n_tr ≈ {n_tr:.2f}e18 cm^-3") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Peak gain versus carrier density. Solid: curves digitised from slide 130 (GaAs 860 nm, InGaAsP 1300 and 1500 nm; approximate). Dashed: free-carrier model for GaAs with no broadening and with 30 meV Gaussian broadening. The model reproduces the sharp onset near transparency, but at a density about 0.3–0.5×10¹⁸ cm⁻³ lower than the measured GaAs curve, and it rises far more steeply.](ld-principle_files/figure-html/fig-peak-gain-output-1.png){#fig-peak-gain width=721 height=391} ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` model transparency density (ΔF = Eg): n_tr ≈ 1.20e18 cm^-3 ``` ::: ::: The free-carrier model shows the physics but overestimates the gain: it neglects the light-hole band, intraband scattering (which broadens each transition by about 10 meV), many-body effects such as bandgap renormalisation, and the polarisation dependence of the matrix element. For design numbers, the slides use measured or fully modelled curves (slide 130), and so does the example of @sec-ld-equation. Near threshold, a **linear** or **logarithmic** fit is common: $$ g_\text{peak}\approx a\,(n-n_{tr})\quad\text{or}\quad g_\text{peak}\approx g_0\ln\frac{n}{n_{tr}}, $$ with the differential gain $a=dg/dn\approx1$–$3\times10^{-16}$ cm² for bulk GaAs and transparency density $n_{tr}\approx1$–$1.5\times10^{18}$ cm⁻³. The differential gain sets the modulation speed (@sec-modulation). ::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"} ## Going further - **Add the light holes.** The valence band has heavy ($m^*\approx0.5m_e$) and light ($m^*\approx0.08m_e$) holes. Compute $E_{Fp}$ with both bands and add the two gain contributions. How much does the transparency density change? - **Gain and spontaneous emission are linked.** The same Fermi factors give the spontaneous spectrum $r_{sp}\propto\alpha_0f_c(1-f_v)$, and $g(h\nu)=r_{sp}(h\nu)\,[1-e^{(h\nu-\Delta F)/k_BT}]\times\text{const}$ (McCumber/van Roosbroeck–Shockley). Measuring the spontaneous spectrum gives the gain (Hakki–Paoli method uses the FP fringes instead). - **Refractive index change.** Gain and refractive index are linked by Kramers–Kronig. The change $dn/dN$ of the index with carrier density causes the **linewidth enhancement factor** $\alpha_H$ and the chirp of directly modulated lasers (@sec-linewidth). ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Complements - M. G. A. Bernard and G. Duraffourg, "Laser conditions in semiconductors", *Phys. Status Solidi* 1, 699 (1961). - Coldren, Corzine and Mašanović, *Diode Lasers and Photonic Integrated Circuits*, 2nd ed. (Wiley, 2012), ch. 4: gain and current relations, with MATLAB code. - Chuang, *Physics of Photonic Devices*, 2nd ed., ch. 9. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. At what injected density does GaAs become transparent for photons at $E_g+10$ meV at 300 K? At 77 K? 2. Why does the gain peak move to shorter wavelength when the current increases (slide 129), while the lasing wavelength of a real laser diode usually moves to longer wavelength (slide 104)? 3. For $n=2\times10^{18}$ cm⁻³ in GaAs, compute the forward voltage needed (ΔF/e). Compare with the 1.5–1.8 V of real diodes. 4. Fit $g=a(n-n_{tr})$ to the digitised GaAs curve of slide 130 between 1.8 and 2.5×10¹⁸ cm⁻³.
